newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: UN funding reform talks with Asia positive -- U.S..
newsitem.headline: UN funding reform talks with Asia positive -- U.S..

text.p: A senior U.S. official said on Wednesday at the end of a tour of five Asian nations that he was optimistic they might help ease Washington's burden in financing the United Nations.
Princeton Lyman told reporters after meeting Singapore officials that the five Asian countries could be asked to pay more in a reform of U.N. funding, an issue Washington is pressing for.

"The general response we've been getting is that there is value in the United Nations being financed more broadly by its members," said Lyman, the acting U.S. assistant secretary of state for international organisation affairs.
Lyman also visited Japan, Malaysia, South Korea and Thailand and said all of them would be prime candidates for increased contributions.
"All these countries are active in the U.N. and probably would be called upon to make greater contributions," he said.
Funding reform would more accurately reflect the economic strength and performance of individual members, something the current formula did not do, Lyman said.
The five nations are part of a group of 60 that contributes 12 percent of U.N. funding, and Lyman said that should change to reflect their new global economic status.
U.S. President Bill Clinton has sent Congress a plan to pay US$1.0 billion that Washington owes the United Nations in dues.

Putting the United Nations on a sounder financial footing was a high priority for the coming year, Lyman said, adding that it was the United States' aim to reduce its contribution to the U.N. budget from 25 percent to 20 percent of the total.
While some of this would be achieved by increased funding from the booming economies of Asia and Latin America, cuts to U.N. programmes would also be inevitable, Lyman said.
"While this is a blunt instrument, there is nothing like cutting your budget to make you prioritise," he said.
Budget cuts of between 10 and 15 percent could be possible in U.N. bodies such as the International Labour Organisation and the World Health Organisation without affecting their work, Lyman said.
"There's room for some kind of efficiency that would make them much more effective on the ground," he said.

Expanding the membership of the Security Council was discussed at the various meetings, but the United States would not support any changes to the veto power of the Council's permanent members, Lyman said.
